extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public and students/scholars of 18th-century English essays
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and commentary from early-18th-century Spectator essays (Addison/Steele) discussing social, linguistic, and cultural prescriptions and observations. The page is a literary-historical edition aimed at general readers and scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in public inscriptions / orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There should be so many gross errors as there are in the very directions of things, wherein accuracy is necessary for the conduct of life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that gross spelling errors on sign-posts and public inscriptions mislead people (example: 'This is the BEER' vs 'This is the BEAR'), cause practical harm (lost dinners, lost way), and are easily amendable. Proposal: tradesmen should pay for upkeep of grammatical correctness; appoint a Swiss Count to remember names. Anti-patterns: painters who render animals poorly and incorrectly spelled signs that mislead strangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility and truthful depiction of shop signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Shop signs must be painted and spelled clearly so the animal or emblem is recognizable to passersby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor painting and incorrect spelling can mislead strangers; the combination of bad painting and bad spelling compounds the problem. Example given: inability to tell the animal on a sign and thus be misled. Proposed remedy: repair and oversight of signs. Scoring note: legible depiction + correct spelling = acceptable; illegible painting or misspelling = failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear distinctions and true characters for place-markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Places and things should be distinguished properly and given true characters to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusion of places (example: mistaking Charing Cross for Stocks Market because of similar statues) can cause mischief. The remedy is better marking and distinctiveness of public monuments and signs. Anti-pattern: erecting similar statues in different places without clear distinguishing markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply literary/witty capacities to public-useful works (public spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of wit should employ their talents on things useful to mankind rather than on abstruse speculations (e.g., emendations of Greek enclitics)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist laments that 'because a thing is everybody's business, it is nobody's business' and advocates public spirit: those with capacities for public service should be employed in works of general use. Anti-pattern: scholars busy with trivial textual emendations while obvious public needs are neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for assuming the title 'Esquire'
rubrics_metrics.description: The title 'Esquire' originally belonged to a particular class: an esquire was a trusty companion of a hero, fit for offices about him (gentle, chaste, active, eloquent); not everyone ought to assume it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author deplores current abuse where clerks and minor persons append 'Esq.' without right. He proposes stricter admission: require certificate of conquest of a lady's heart, ability to lead a country dance, carry messages with secrecy and diligence, and signatures by 'three toasts, and one prude' before receiving the title. Anti-patterns: indiscriminate use of 'Esq.' in office superscriptions and among rural 'esquires' lacking the manners and accomplishments described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence of Heralds' Office in verifying arms and appellations
rubrics_metrics.description: Heralds should properly understand their duties and prevent the promiscuous and absurd admission of persons into the order of Esquires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negligence by heralds leads to the jumbled misuse of titles; better enforcement and knowledge by heralds would curb innovations and impostures. Example: foreigners using naturalisation as pretext to assume titles. Scoring note: proper heraldic verification = social order preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and provision for decayed news-writers (veterans)
rubrics_metrics.description: News-writers who served the public in wartime deserve institutional support after peace (analogous to military pensions/hospitals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because peace will leave many news-writers without employment (they supplied wars with plentiful 'news'), the author proposes adding apartments with pen, ink, paper, and sustenance to the Hospital of Chelsea for decayed news-writers, who could compile annals of veterans. Anti-pattern: leaving veteran journalists 'broken' with no provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical performance criterion: 'proper action' can redeem weak dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: In plays with inferior dialogue, skilled acting and 'proper action' can make characters (e.g., a young man of fortune) acceptable and engaging to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The Trip to the Jubilee' — though dialogue low, Mr. Wilks' action supplies gallantry and gaiety. Performance quality (action, physical portrayal) is a critical evaluative dimension and can compensate for textual shortcomings. Anti-pattern: relying solely on dialogue without effective stage action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal sufficiency for divorce claims: plain representation required
rubrics_metrics.description: To seek legal redress (divorce), the complainant must represent causes plainly and candidly; suspicions or guesses (even if true) are insufficient for formal suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative advises that without explicit stated causes, a lawyer cannot advise or pursue a case; public trials bring mortifications and the law gives no remedy for infirmity due only to age. Anti-pattern: expecting law to act on vague suspicions or transient complaints; inability to provide explicit grounds will defeat suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue of self-denial within matrimony as social/casuistic standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Curbing desires (self-denial) is presented as the greatest worldly glory and a virtue that may argue against public legal action for private grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author counsels patience and self-restraint in matrimony as morally preferable to airing grievances publicly; examples cited of women living happily secluded or remaining chaste into advanced age. Anti-pattern: immediate recourse to public litigation for private sexual dissatisfaction without weighing virtue and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theater profession and public benefit: theatrical profits for public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing as a trade is acceptable when it contributes to public benefit (theater profits maintaining a hospital); professions should not make individuals excessively rich at public expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Amsterdam theatre actors are tradesmen earning modest pay and profits sustain a hospital; contrast with the idea that English playhouses might also found charitable institutions (Dulwich hospital by Alleyn). Implicit evaluative standard: artistic professions should serve commonwealth benefits rather than private enrichment.
